analysis.one_liner: Forces agencies to repeal two existing rules before issuing any new rule that adds business costs.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a single committee action: it was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The RED Tape Act would impose a "two-for-one" rule on federal agencies: an agency could not issue any new rule that adds a financial or administrative burden on businesses or people unless it first repealed or amended at least two existing burden-creating rules, and the new rule's cost could not exceed the cost of the rules it replaced [S2] [S3]. The agency head would personally determine and certify which rules count as burdens and what they cost [S3]. The bill died in committee with no cosponsors and no votes [S4] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses that bear the cost of complying with federal rules would gain, because every new protective rule would require two existing rules to be removed first, capping the total cost of regulation. The bill's stated purpose is reducing the cumulative burden of regulation [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: No agency could issue a rule that adds a new financial or administrative burden unless it repealed or amended at least two existing burden-creating rules, and the new rule had to cost no more than the ones removed [S2] [S3].
Agencies would have to publish semiannual lists of rules they plan to issue or repeal, with the cost of each, and could not issue a covered rule without doing so [S3].

Before repealing a rule, agencies would weigh whether the rule achieved its purpose, whether it became obsolete, whether its costs outweigh its benefits, and whether repeal would cause adverse effects [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public that relies on federal protections would bear the cost. Rules on air and water pollution, workplace safety, consumer finance, food safety, and more all impose compliance burdens, so any of them could be forcibly traded away to clear room for an unrelated new rule. The determination of what counts as a burden, and what rules cost, would rest with the agency head, so the arithmetic would be decided by the same officials under pressure to keep the count moving [S3].

drawbacks.text: The two-for-one formula is mechanical: it does not compare the value of the new rule to the value of the two rules being removed. A low-cost new rule could force repeal of two higher-value protections in an unrelated area [S3].
The agency head, not an independent body, determines which rules count as creating a burden and certifies their costs, so the constraint operates only as tightly as the agency itself chooses [S3].

Supporters would counter that rules accumulate over decades, some become obsolete, and a hard budget forces agencies to prioritize and prune, though the bill's own repeal criteria already let agencies judge each rule on its merits without a mandatory two-for-one trade [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Regulatory accumulation is a real phenomenon and the bill's goals of repealing obsolete and overlapping rules have merit, but the bill does not achieve them in a targeted way. Its core mechanism is a rigid quota that treats every rule's cost as equivalent and every repeal as a fair trade, and it leaves the key determinations to the agency head. For a bill that would apply across environmental, safety, consumer, and financial regulation, the risks to existing protections outweigh the pruning benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dan Sullivan introduced the bill on February 12, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs [S1] [S5].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded — and the bill expired with the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who rely on federal protections for clean air and water, workplace safety, consumer finance, and food safety are better off that the bill never advanced, since a mandatory two-for-one repeal quota would have put those protections on the auction block. Businesses hoping for a hard cap on regulatory cost gains nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People relying on federal regulatory protections

sides.party_line_note: The bill never came to a vote, and it drew no cosponsors from either party, so no party position is on the record [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would cap the total cost any agency can impose, requiring two burden-creating rules to be removed for every new one, which would systematically limit new protections across health, safety, consumer, and environmental regulation [S2] [S3]. Compliance savings for business would come at the expense of the public benefits the displaced rules provided.
Agencies would lose discretion to issue new rules freely but gain a structured process for clearing outdated rules from their books, with the agency head deciding the key cost determinations [S3].
